title: Letter II
focus: loneliness and the desire for a friend

teacherSummary.text: From Archangel, Walton hires a ship and crew but confesses that he has no friend who shares his enthusiasm. He describes his master and lieutenant and promises Margaret he will not 'kill the albatross.'

context.history: Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798), alluded to here, was hugely popular; Mary Shelley heard Coleridge recite it as a child.

significance: Walton's loneliness introduces the novel's central need: companionship. The albatross allusion warns of punishment for violating nature.
discussionQuestions: Why does Walton feel he needs a friend, and what kind of friend does he want?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with nature versus nurture?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Letter II,” how does Shelley show loneliness and the desire for a friend? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Letter II develops the idea of loneliness and the desire for a friend. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses characterization in Letter II to complicate the reader's understanding of loneliness and the desire for a friend. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Letter II within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of loneliness and the desire for a friend responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Letter II as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of loneliness and the desire for a friend. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Why does Walton feel he needs a friend, and what kind of friend does he want? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include albatross, embarkation, amassed, unemployed, endowments. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “I am going to unexplored regions, to “the land of mist and snow”; but I shall kill no albatross, therefore do not be alarmed for my safety, or if I should come back to you as worn and woeful as the “Ancient Mariner.”” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: A web-footed bird, of the genus Diomedea, of which there are several species.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798), alluded to here, was hugely popular; Mary Shelley heard Coleridge recite it as a child. Now, why does this chapter matter? Walton's loneliness introduces the novel's central need: companionship. The albatross allusion warns of punishment for violating nature. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
